candidates.context: In general, the purposes of a PMR under section 505(o)(3) are related to serious risks. The term 106 serious risk is defined for purposes of section 505(o) as a risk of a serious adverse drug 107 experience . This description does not mean that such postmarketing studies and clinical trials 108 are limited to safety endpoints. Rather, in some cases, a postmarketing study or clinical trial 109 with efficacy endpoints may be appropriate, for example, to further assess whether a potential 110 lack of expected pharmacological effect, including reduced effectiveness, may result in a serious 111 adverse drug experience. 16 Under section 506B of the FD&C Act and 21 CFR 314.81(b)(2)(vii) and 601.70, applicants are 117 required to report annually on the status of certain PMRs and PMCs, including PMRs required 118 under section 505(o)(3) of the FD&C Act. Postmarketing Adverse Event Reports and the FDA’s Adverse Event Reporting 191 Systems 192 Section 505(k)(1) of the FD&C Act describes data that the applicant must report to FDA relating 194 to clinical experience and other data or information associated with drugs. 22 The regulations 195 implementing section 505(k)(1) include, among other things, a requirement for applicants to 196 submit adverse event information, electronically, to FDA. The FDA Adverse Event Reporting 197 System (FAERS) and Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) databases 23 contain 198 individual case safety reports (ICSRs) that applicants submit based on information provided by 199 consumers, patients, and health care providers. candidates.statement: For example, evaluation of a specific safety concern may need to be assessed within both the 333 intended general population and a subpopulation. FDA may require an applicant to conduct a 334 postmarketing study or clinical trial to assess a serious risk in a specific subpopulation that 335 cannot be identified in ARIA and FDA may perform its own assessment of the same safety 336 concern in the general population using the ARIA system. In this example, FDA would issue a 337 PMR focusing on the specific subpopulation but would not issue a PMR for the related 338 assessment of the safety concern in the general population. The combination of the information 339 obtained from the postmarketing study or clinical trial performed by the applicant with the 340 information FDA obtains from its own assessment within ARIA would provide a more 341 comprehensive understanding of the serious risk at issue. 342
candidates.context: Even after requiring that an applicant conduct a postmarketing study or clinical trial for a 326 particular purpose, FDA may also perform ARIA analyses as part of its pharmacovigilance 327 activities for a drug to further evaluate the drug’s safety. That is, even if the FDA considers the 328 ARIA system insufficient to adequately address a specific serious risk (based upon the 329 considerations above) and a PMR is issued, the ARIA system may still play a role in 330 understanding a broader or related aspect of the issue. 331 5. candidates.context: Such studies are generally designed to assess a serious risk associated with a drug 420 exposure or quantify risk or evaluate factors that affect this risk (e.g., drug dose, timing of 421 exposure, patient characteristics). Data sources for observational studies could include 422 administrative health care claims data, electronic medical records, registries, 423 prospectively collected observational data, or other sources of observational information. 424 — To facilitate interpretation of the findings, the studies should always have protocols 429 (including a statistical analysis plan), should include control groups, and should test 430 prespecified hypotheses. A control group may be omitted when there is a 431 scientifically valid reason. 432

candidates.statement: FDA has authority to enforce the section 505(o)(3)(E)(ii) requirements for postmarketing studies 668 and clinical trials. 34 An applicant’s failure to comply with the timetable, periodic report 669 submissions, and other requirements of section 505(o)(3)(E)(ii) of the FD&C Act will be 670 considered a violation unless the applicant demonstrates good cause for the noncompliance. 671 Section 505(o)(3)(E)(ii) of the FD&C Act provides that FDA shall determine what constitutes 672 good cause. In addition, under section 505(p)(2) of the FD&C Act, failure to conduct a 673 postmarketing study or clinical trial required under section 506B of the FD&C Act and subparts 674 H and E (21 CFR 314.510 and 601.41) may result in enforcement action. 675

candidates.statement: • Misbranding charges. A drug is misbranded under section 502(z) of the FD&C Act (21 684 U.S.C. 332(z)) if the applicant for that drug violates postmarketing study or clinical trial 685 requirements, including those outlined in section II.B., Applicants Are Required to 686 Report on the Status of Studies and Clinical Trials. 687
candidates.context: • Charges under section 505 of the FD&C Act. A responsible person 35 may not introduce 679 or deliver into interstate commerce the drug involved if the person is in violation of 680 section 505(o) (postmarketing study and clinical trial requirements) (see section 681 505(o)(1) of the FD&C Act) or 505(p)(2) (certain postmarketing studies). 682 • Civil monetary penalties. Under section 303(f)(4)(A) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 689 333(f)(4)(A)), an applicant that violates postmarketing study or clinical trial requirements 690 may be subject to civil monetary penalties of up to $250,000 per violation, but no more 691 than $1 million for all violations adjudicated in a single proceeding. These penalties 692 increase if the violation continues more than 30 days after FDA notifies the applicant of 693 the violation.
